headline: New Phobia Identified: 'Fear That Your Personal Data Is Bored'
subheadline: Psychologists document growing anxiety about unstimulated information
summary: Psychologists have identified a new form of digital anxiety: concern that one's personal data isn't being used interestingly enough.
content:
Psychologists have documented a new form of digital-age anxiety: the fear that your personal data, sitting in corporate servers, is bored.

The phenomenon, tentatively named "data ennui anxiety," manifests as concern that the information collected about you isn't being used in interesting or meaningful ways.

"I know they have all my data," explained one sufferer. "My browsing history, my purchases, my location data. And what are they doing with it? Showing me ads for things I already bought. It feels like a waste. My data deserves better."

The anxiety appears to stem from the disconnect between the perceived intrusiveness of data collection and the mundane applications of that data. Users who expected surveillance state levels of analysis are disappointed to discover their information is used primarily to sell them slightly more relevant sneakers.

"I thought they were building a profile of me," said another sufferer. "I thought they understood me on some deep level. Then I got an ad for cat food. I don't have a cat. They don't even know me. All that data and they don't even know me."

Psychologists note this represents a novel inversion of privacy concerns. "Usually people are worried about being watched," explained Dr. Patricia Huang. "These individuals are worried about being watched poorly. They want their surveillance to be competent."

Symptoms include checking targeted ads for "signs of understanding," disappointment when recommendations are generic, and a vague sense that "my data could be doing so much more."

"I gave them everything," one patient reportedly said. "And they're just... not using it well. It's sitting there. Bored. I can feel my data getting bored."

Treatment approaches are still being developed. One therapist has suggested "radical acceptance that algorithms don't care about you personally." Results have been mixed.

At press time, 847 people had self-diagnosed after reading this article.
author: Sandra Mitchell, Technology & Psychology
